label: How Python Pathways works
lines: Hi, and welcome to Python Pathways! Let me show you how it all works.
First, you sign up once. You'll give your name, your school email, your grade, your teacher and your level, and you'll pick a secret four-digit PIN.
Next time you come back, just type your name and your PIN, and you'll carry on exactly where you stopped.
Every lesson follows the same path. Watch the video, read the Learn page, try the example, solve three exercises, and then practise.
Write your code, then press Check. Every exercise you get right earns you ten points.
Stuck? You can buy some advice for five points. So use your points wisely.
Now, House Points. Finish your exercises, that's fifteen on Beginner, ten on Intermediate or five on Advanced, and work for at least thirty minutes. You can earn one each session.
When you earn a House Point, Submit unlocks, and you can send your work to your teacher.
A few things to know. Finished exercises can't be redone, each lesson lasts forty minutes, and please keep your PIN to yourself.
That's it. You're ready. Let's write some code!

label: Criterion A: Inquiring and analysing
paras: Welcome to MYP Design, year 1. This is Criterion A: Inquiring and analysing. Our unit is Smart & Sustainable City 2050.

In Criterion A you investigate the problem before you design anything. You find out why it is a problem and who it affects, plan and prioritise your research, and finish with a design brief that decides what you will make.
Your own design challenge is on the screen now. Read it carefully, because this is the problem you will be solving.

Strand i. Understand the problem: why it is a problem, who it affects and why it has not been solved. Explain the problem in depth: what is happening, why it matters, who it affects, why nobody has solved it, and what happens if nothing changes. Back every fact with a source.

Strand ii. List the research questions that will help you understand the problem and the need for a solution. Write the questions you need answered to understand the problem. Mix primary questions (you find out) and secondary questions (others have published), and ask about existing products.
Strand iii. Justify each research question and prioritise them. For every question, say why you need the answer and where you will find it, then rank it High, Medium or Low.

Strand iv. Develop a design brief from your research, using ACCESS FM. Answer your key questions, then decide what you will design. Describe it with ACCESS FM: Aesthetics, Cost, Client, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Materials.

You will be marked out of 8. To reach the top band, 7 to 8: You describe the problem in depth: why it is a problem, who it affects and why it has not been solved, supported by sourced facts and examples. You list a full range of relevant primary and secondary research questions (6+), justify each one and prioritise them clearly. Your detailed design brief is built on your research findings and covers every part of ACCESS FM.

Next, study the worked example. It uses a different problem, so you learn the method without copying. Then read the method and the rubric, pass the practice, and complete your own task, strand by strand. Good luck, designer!

label: Criterion B: Developing ideas
paras: Welcome to MYP Design, year 1. This is Criterion B: Developing ideas. Our unit is Smart & Sustainable City 2050.
In Criterion B you turn your design brief into a specification, design your product in different looks, find out which design principles your client likes, and develop your final design.
Your own design challenge is on the screen now. Read it carefully, because this is the problem you will be solving.
Strand i. Develop a design specification from your design brief. Turn your design brief into specific, measurable requirements. Each one must be something you can test later.

Strand ii. Present a range of design ideas: the same product in different looks, labelled and annotated. Design the SAME product in different looks: same content, different layout, colours, fonts or style. Label and annotate everything.
Strand iii. Identify the design principles the client likes in each design, with reasons. Show your designs to your client. Record which design principles they like from each one and why.
Strand iv. Develop the final design from the best ideas. Combine the best principles into one final, detailed design. Show which idea came from which design.

You will be marked out of 8. To reach the top band, 7 to 8: You develop a detailed specification (6+ points) in which every requirement is specific, measurable and linked to your brief. You present at least 2 clear, accurate designs of the same product in genuinely different looks, fully labelled and annotated. You describe the design principles chosen from each design using the client's feedback. Your developed design is accurate and detailed, shows where each idea came from, and lists everything needed to make it.

Next, study the worked example. It uses a different problem, so you learn the method without copying. Then read the method and the rubric, pass the practice, and complete your own task, strand by strand. Good luck, designer!

label: Criterion C: Creating the solution
paras: Welcome to MYP Design, year 1. This is Criterion C: Creating the solution. Our unit is Smart & Sustainable City 2050.
In Criterion C you write a SMART step-by-step plan, use your technical skills to build your developed design, check that you followed your plan, and justify any changes.
Your own design challenge is on the screen now. Read it carefully, because this is the problem you will be solving.

Strand i. Write a logical plan: a SMART, step-by-step instruction manual. Write an instruction manual so clear that a classmate could build your developed design from it. Every step must be specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and timed.

Strand ii. Demonstrate technical skills by creating the solution. Build your solution, following your plan. Capture evidence at every stage: the quality of your technical skills is what is assessed here.
Strand iii. Follow the logical plan to create the solution. Check each step of your plan against your making evidence. Did you follow it accurately?
Strand iv. Justify the changes made to the design and plan. Record anything that changed from your brief, specification or plan, why it changed, and its effect.

You will be marked out of 8. To reach the top band, 7 to 8: Your logical plan is a SMART, step-by-step instruction manual (8+ steps) that a classmate could follow exactly. You show excellent technical skills, with clear evidence at each stage. You follow your plan accurately, and your solution works as intended. You list and explain every change that was not in your brief, specification or plan.

Next, study the worked example. It uses a different problem, so you learn the method without copying. Then read the method and the rubric, pass the practice, and complete your own task, strand by strand. Good luck, designer!

label: Criterion D: Evaluating
paras: Welcome to MYP Design, year 1. This is Criterion D: Evaluating. Our unit is Smart & Sustainable City 2050.
In Criterion D you test your solution against your specification, record the evidence, suggest improvements for anything that failed, and present your improved solution and its impact.
Your own design challenge is on the screen now. Read it carefully, because this is the problem you will be solving.
Strand i. Write a test plan: test name, specification, method and expected result. Plan a test for every specification point: give each test a name, a method and the result you expect.

Strand ii. Test the solution and record the testing evidence. Carry out every test. Record the expected result, the actual result, the outcome, pass or fail, and whether the result is qualitative or quantitative.
Strand iii. Suggest an improvement for each failure. Look at what failed or could be better, and suggest a specific improvement for each.
Strand iv. Present the improved solution and explain its impact on the client. Show your solution improved, explain how the improvements fix the failures, and describe the impact on your client.

You will be marked out of 8. To reach the top band, 7 to 8: Your test plan covers every specification point (4+ tests) with clear methods and measurable expected results. Your testing evidence is complete and accurate, with outcomes, pass or fail, and qualitative or quantitative data. Every failure has a specific, realistic improvement. You present an improved solution that shows the improvements working, and describe its impact on the client and users.

Next, study the worked example. It uses a different problem, so you learn the method without copying. Then read the method and the rubric, pass the practice, and complete your own task, strand by strand. Good luck, designer!
